claims.text: An OOPSLA 2025 empirical evaluation of Python projects using mutation testing found each property-based test caught about 50 times as many mutations as the average unit test (odds ratio 52 after controlling for coverage), and only 15% of mutations were found by both kinds of test.

In a study of 16 HumanEval problems where standard solutions failed extended tests, Claude-4-sonnet-generated property-based tests and example-based tests each detected bugs in 11 of 16 cases (68.75%), and combining them detected 13 of 16 (81.25%).
In the Property-Generated Solver paper, property-based-testing feedback raised repair success on initially failed LiveCodeBench problems to 75.9%, versus 46.6% when feedback came from public tests.
Four LLM calls at 95% individual stability yield roughly 81% system-level stability, so unit-level property tests miss failures that emerge from multi-step composition.

GPT-4 as a judge matched human preferences with over 80% agreement, but Claude-v1 favoured the first position 75% of the time, and GPT-4 and Claude-v1 favoured their own outputs by 10% and 25% higher win rates respectively.
On JudgeBench, which uses harder reasoning, knowledge, math and coding pairs, vanilla GPT-4o scored 50.86% as a judge, close to random guessing.

A benchmark of 54 LLM judges against 1,994 expert-annotated samples found 36 passed a correlation screen of r ≥ 0.80 but only 27 reached Tier 1 human-like agreement, so correlation alone is insufficient.
Airbnb's faithfulness LLM judge agreed with a product manager only 78% of the time because it penalised accurate paraphrases; rubric changes and few-shot examples raised agreement to 88%.

In a 900-session experiment with 30 artifacts and 150 planted errors, cross-model review did not differ significantly in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session, though the two found partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%).

In the same cross-model experiment, the best cross-model condition (GPT-5.4 reviewer, 32.3% F1) was not significantly better than cross-context review (28.6%; adjusted p = 1.00), and 14 cross-model sessions failed.

A practitioner brief concludes cross-model review should be used as a challenge rather than an approval, and that architectural changes, public API shifts, migrations and sensitive security logic should stay in the human-review lane.
On Macroscope's own 118-bug benchmark, bug catch rates were Macroscope 48.3%, CodeRabbit 45.8%, Cursor Bugbot 42.4%, Greptile 23.6% and Graphite Diamond 18.3%.
Greptile's own comparison on 50 open-source pull requests claims it catches over 50% more bugs than CodeRabbit, which conflicts with the vendor-run Macroscope benchmark.

Google's AutoCommenter initially placed 80% of comments on lines the author had not modified, and its useful-comment ratio plateaued at 54% by developer feedback and 60% by independent raters before suppressing non-actionable rules raised it to 66% and 74%.
Meta's TestGen-LLM produced test cases of which 75% built correctly, 57% passed reliably and 25% increased coverage, and 73% of its recommendations were accepted for production.
Anthropic's April 2026 Claude Code postmortem found a verbosity limit passed internal testing yet caused a 3% quality drop, because the eval suite was too narrow to detect it.
Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench until grading bugs (such as penalising '96.12' when expecting '96.124991…') were fixed, after which its score rose to 95%.
In τ-bench, GPT-4o with function calling succeeded on under 50% of tasks, with pass^8 below 25% in retail, showing strong inconsistency across repeated trials.
In τ²-bench, GPT-4.1's pass^1 dropped from 74% (retail) and 56% (airline) to 34% on telecom with dual control, and user-simulator error rates were 40% in retail and 47% in airline.
SPADE's assertion synthesis reduced assertion count by 14% and false failure rate by 21% versus baselines across nine real LLM pipelines.
In a comparison of assertion generators, EvalGen reached 0.73 defect recall versus SPADE's 0.49 on a product task.

Traversaal lists signals of eval overfitting: eval scores diverging from production reliability, every sprint closing with 'fixed failing evals', engineers predicting which cases fail next, and holdout performance being unknown or worse than the active suite.
Parasoft claims its Virtualize service virtualization yields 33% more defects found in QA and test and a 74% decrease in the critical defect escape ratio (vendor-reported).
Keploy's vendor comparison claims traffic-recorded tests and mocks reach 90% coverage from the first recording and 94% of production paths, versus 16% for manually written tests.
Multi-agent debate improved accuracy in the cited study from 66% to 74% on biography generation, 64% to 71% on MMLU, 67% to 82% on arithmetic and 74% to 100% on chess move optimality.
